He taught us, as a species, that all new learning, with the exception of some motor skills, passes through, and is regulated by, this small part of the brain. And this has turned out to be one of the biggest misses in education and training for centuries. Education and training have basically always focused on the moment of epiphany or new understanding. But it turns out that encoding, storing, and retrieving new information require energy, and energy is in short supply in our brains. So, an additional layer, beyond the parts of the brain engaged in having the moment of epiphany, evolved to make a judgment about whether that new understanding would have future value and should be stored in enduring memory or quickly forgotten. And as we eventually uncovered, sometimes, the teaching optimization strategies for gaining an epiphany are in direct conflict with the rules used by the hippocampus to determine whether to store that insight. Let me give you an example. If you are teaching and you ask a learner a question, and they are confident in their answer but also wrong, epiphany-priority focused teaching calls that a “teaching moment,” or sometimes, the “hypercorrection effect.” So, we were all trained to give the answer right away. And while it is true that this has a strong correlation with having the epiphany, it has a negative correlation with the actual creation of enduring memory. It is as if the hippocampus says, “I see that every time I need the answer, it is given to me in real time, so there is no need to spend the energy required to rewire that new knowledge into enduring synaptic memory.” We tested this extensively, and it turns out that if you simply acknowledge that the answer is wrong and move on to another question or two and then come back to the answer that was missed, the hippocampus tends to prioritize this knowledge, as if saying, “I remember missing that; I’d better store it.” How many times have you had an interesting epiphany and only days later could not remember what it was? That is because your hippocampus determined it was not worth storing. Removing Henry’s hippocampus instantly turned off his ability to learn. And as we will explore, that also turned off his ability to have a persistent conscious experience of life. While he was conscious in each moment, without memory creation, he had no persistent sense of his life. This will play back into how we manage memory in AI systems. Scientists studied Henry’s brain for more than fifty years, during which time he lived without the ability to form new memories, and in a final act of generosity, his brain was donated to science after his death in 2008. Researchers at the MIND Institute at UC San Diego performed a painstaking fifty-three-hour procedure to section and preserve it. 10 The entire process was digitally imaged at microscopic resolution, resulting in more than 2,400 slices and a complete three-dimensional reconstruction of his brain. In the deepest irony, the man who could not form new memories became the foundation for how we understand memory itself. The Advent of the Functional fMRI Thirty-eight years after Henry’s original brain surgery, we were given a tool to peer into the brain and advance our understanding of human learning. The year was 1992. At Massachusetts General Hospital, a young researcher named Kenneth Kwong, PhD, was part of a team working on a new imaging technique that used magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) not just to take static pictures of the brain’s structure but to watch it work dynamically while interacting. The breakthrough hinged on a surprising fact: When neurons fire, they consume oxygen, and the blood flow in that region increases slightly to compensate. This change in blood oxygenation could be detected using a variant of MRI known as BOLD contrast—blood oxygen level dependent imaging. And with that, the functional MRI (fMRI) was born. Kwong’s paper, published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , became a cornerstone in modern neuroscience. 11 It was like Galileo turning his telescope to the stars—only this time, we were looking inward. Also at Harvard, Daniel Schacter, PhD, used the fMRI to explore the architecture of memory and its malfunctions. His acclaimed book The Seven Sins of Memory reframed forgetting not as failure but as adaptation: a system optimized to remember what matters, not everything. 12 In Schacter’s view, when memory distorts or forgets, it isn’t failing—it’s revealing the trade-offs of a system built not for perfect recall but for adaptive reconstruction and forward-looking efficiency, optimized to operate within the constraints of attention, relevance, and cognitive bandwidth. The constraints of having only twenty watts of energy. Meanwhile, at Washington University in St. Louis, Henry “Roddy” Roediger III, PhD, led pioneering studies in retrieval-based learning and memory consolidation, later captured in the acclaimed book Make It Stick . 13 Since 2011, I have had the great honor to benefit from the work of both Schacter and Roediger through their work on the science advisory board of the advanced learning company we built. And memory wasn’t the only frontier. In 2016, researchers using ultra-high-field fMRI revealed how our brains process predictions and reality in layered circuits—with top-down expectations and bottom-up input activating different layers of the visual cortex. We will take a look at this later in our exploration, because it turns out to be core to how artificial intelligence learns and builds its own model of the world. These discoveries hinted at something profound: a hyperefficient layered prediction engine inside the human brain that would become central to AI’s breakout.
